source.title: Debate Helps Weak-to-Strong Generalization
source.authors: Hao Lang; Fei Huang; Yong-Bin Li

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It uses the weak-to-strong fine-tuning pipeline and PGR measure, and reports a naive weak-label fine-tuning baseline alongside modified methods.
record.gate_note: The PGR values in Tables 2, 4 and 5 are recorded. Figures 2 and 3 report final accuracy trends for ensemble size and debate turns, but do not report PGR, so they are not rows for the versions tested here.
record.test_reason: The study uses the OpenAI weak-to-strong codebase, PGR and its NLP datasets with a Qwen-7B supervisor and a Qwen-14B student. It reports naive weak-label fine-tuning (V1), the original confidence-loss variants, and new debate and ensemble supervision methods (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right: the authors conclude that debate, combined with debate ensembles, builds a better weak supervisor and raises PGR on all four tasks, and that all student PGRs are positive. The paraphrase should add that the authors say confidence losses give a modest boost. Their own Table 2 contradicts this: those losses are equal to or below naive on 5 of 8 comparisons. The authors attribute this to the small 7B-to-14B compute gap.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original weak-to-strong pipeline and PGR, but augments weak-model training with strong-model debate transcripts and weak-model ensembles. The weak and strong pretrained models are Qwen/Qwen-7B and Qwen/Qwen-14B.
record.method_sensitivity: PGR differs across tasks and training variants; debate-ensemble results exceed single weak-model and finetune-ensemble results in all four datasets.
record.problems: The weak-to-strong size gap is only 7B versus 14B, and the authors note that this may limit performance and that their conclusions need checking on larger, more advanced models. The reported experiments are in NLP only. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2 and 3 are omitted because they report accuracy rather than PGR; the text describes ensemble-cardinality trends and declining accuracy beyond three debate turns.

untested.parts: Only one size pair (Qwen-7B to Qwen-14B) and binary NLP classification.
Only one supervisor/student size pair. Four tasks are reported but task dependence and its predictors are not analysed. No chess, reward modelling or representation analysis.

missing.what: Per-task weak and strong-ceiling accuracies (e.g. AnthropicHH 48.8 / 50.8), needed to judge PGR robustness. They are absent from the row baselines.
missing.locator: Table 2, Weak performance and Strong ceiling rows

missing.what: The accuracy of the debate-enhanced weak ensemble supervisor is not reported, so whether the student beats its own supervisor under debate cannot be read. This is a gap in the paper, not a row omission.

record.verdict_notes: In this study PGR always uses the naive small model as the weak reference, even for debate-enhanced supervisors. Debate, consultancy and ensemble rows therefore measure gain over naive weak-to-strong (V2), not the student exceeding its own supervisor (V1). Rows R19, R22, R25, R28, R31, R34, R37 and R40 duplicate R4, R8, R12 and R16. No seeds or uncertainty are reported, and several PGR differences correspond to 0.1-0.3 accuracy points. AnthropicHH accuracies are near 50%. The V3 links were dropped because task variation is reported but not analysed.

versions.untested_parts: No settings beyond the reported NLP classification tasks and Qwen/Qwen-7B to Qwen/Qwen-14B setup.
The paper tests debate-based supervision, weak-model ensembles and the listed confidence-loss variants; it does not test every possible loss variant or training change.
Task variation is tested across four NLP datasets. Size variation beyond the single 7B-to-14B pairing, chess, reward modelling, and representation-based predictors are not tested.
Distribution shift, shared errors between weak and strong models, and exploiting what a weak supervisor cannot check are not tested.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are tested.
